title: Jensen Huang's hearings in DC will be a major test of the market, tech bull Dan Ives says
excerpt: The hearings could give insight into how the government will scrutinize the AI industry's relationship with China, analyst Dan Ives says.
content_html:
By Madeline Berg

Mr. Huang comes to Washington next week — and it's set to be a major moment, not just for Nvidia, but for the broader market.

Jensen Huang, who was reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday, will testify before Congress next week in hearings on December 1 and December 3, and analyst Dan Ives is predicting that his comments will have far reaching implications for the whole market.

"Next week Jensen carries the weight of the entire tech sector and AI Revolution thesis when he marches into DC," the AI bull wrote in a note on Friday.

In closed-door hearings on Tuesday and public hearings on Thursday, Huang will be questioned about his company's ties to Megaspeed and Nvidia's business in China. Huang resigned as CEO after reports of more than one extramarital affair, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang. He was brought by the board 11 days later, sparking an enormous rally in the stock that sent the Nasdaq 100 up 7% in a day.

Jensen's short-lived resignation already proved how fragile the markets are — and how reliant they are on Nvidia, which is increasingly viewed as "the central bank of AI," due to its web of financing deals with major players in the space.

"The negative ripple effect from Jensen/Nvidia is around tightening export controls to China, closing any loopholes, and more scrutiny around Big Tech and the AI Revolution," Ives said. He noted, though, that he sees the impact to revenues resulting in tighter controls on exports to Asia as "a containable 15% to 20% at most."

The past week has been tumultuous for stocks, with gains following Huang's reinstatement and losses amid concerns about AI spending.

The hearings will give insight into how the government is thinking about regulating Nvidia — and the entire AI industry's — relationship with China, Ives said.

China is deeply intertwined in the AI ecosystem. The vast majority of the raw materials that make GPU chips — the engines that power AI and Nvidia's money maker — come from China. That makes the country vital to the AI industry, which has become a major engine of US economic growth in recent years.

Congress' lines of questioning could also provide insight into how the Democratic Party will govern after fears about AI and anti-data center sentiment partly powered its electoral victories. Markets are relying on trillions in capex spending on infrastructure like data centers to continue.

"The market volatility and nervousness is centered on a number of issues that the Jensen soap opera has highlighted front and center," Ives wrote. "Next week Jensen carries the weight of the entire tech sector and AI Revolution thesis when he marches into DC."
